memory_update.text: AIR should be carried forward as a high-relevance underfollowed aviation-capacity candidate: parts supply, MRO, repair engineering, and software map directly to aircraft availability and maintenance-turnaround constraints.

AGYS should be carried forward as a niche hospitality operating-software candidate: exposure is indirect but potentially strong if labor scarcity and complex resort/hotel/cruise operations require embedded PMS/POS/inventory systems.
ABM should be tracked as an airport labor and passenger-throughput services candidate; next layer must isolate Aviation segment economics and wage-inflation sensitivity.
OSK is less pure but has a specific airport-equipment chokepoint angle through Oshkosh AeroTech; keep only if AeroTech contribution/backlog is material enough to affect consolidated results.

Need additional search for US-listed or ADR airport operators, baggage-handling automation vendors, ground-handling pure plays, travel-experience infrastructure operators, and specialty hospitality distributors. Many direct ground handlers and baggage-system vendors appear private or non-US-listed.

Layer 1B evidence supports the hypothesis that travel capacity constraints are not limited to consumer demand: maintenance slots, parts availability, airport labor, gate equipment, baggage systems, and hospitality workflow software are plausible second-order pressure points.
